title: 1st Grade Subtraction Word Problems: The 3 Story Types (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: 1st Grade Subtraction Word Problems + Free Quiz
meta_desc: The three kinds of 1st grade subtraction word problems a six-year-old meets, a read-underline-solve-check method, examples within 20 and a free quiz.
excerpt: Not every subtraction story means take-away. There are three kinds a first-grader meets, and the trickiest ones don't feel like subtraction at all. Here are the three, a four-step method, and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Read this to a six-year-old: ‘Priya had 12 toffees. She gave 5 to her brother. How many are left?’ Most will happily count back to 7. Now try this one: ‘Rohan has 12 marbles and Sameer has 8. How many more does Rohan have?’ Same subtraction — 12 − 8 — but watch the pause. Nothing was given away, nothing left the group, so it does not feel like subtraction at all. That gap, between the arithmetic and the story, is what 1st grade subtraction word problems really test. And most subtraction stories a first-grader meets are one of just three kinds.

Here is the catch parents rarely hear: only one of the three is the familiar take-away. The other two look nothing like it, which is exactly why children who can rattle off 12 − 5 still stall on a story. Below are the three types, a four-step method that fits on one hand, and worked examples kept within 20 the way the NCERT Grade 1 syllabus expects.

The three kinds of subtraction stories a six-year-old meets

Teachers call these problem structures, but your child does not need the jargon. They need to hear enough of each type to recognise its shape when it turns up.

1. Take-away stories (something leaves the group)

Something starts, then part of it goes. ‘Priya had 12 toffees; she gave away 5.’ There is a clear before and after, and the group shrinks. These are the easiest to see as subtraction, because the action — giving, eating, losing, spending — feels like taking away. Start every child here.

2. Compare stories (how many more, how many fewer)

This is the one that catches children out. ‘Rohan has 12 marbles, Sameer has 8. How many more does Rohan have?’ Nothing moves and nobody loses anything — you are lining the two amounts up and measuring the gap between them. The gap is 12 − 8 = 4. Children who have only met take-away freeze here, because there is no action to picture. I spend the most time on compare stories; get the habit right early and it saves years of trouble.

3. Missing-part stories (how many more are needed)

A total is known and one part is known; the other part is missing. ‘Aarav needs 15 stickers to fill his chart. He has 9. How many more does he need?’ A child’s instinct is often to add, because ‘how many more’ sounds like growing — but you are finding the missing piece, and 15 − 9 = 6 gives it. These stories quietly build the link between subtraction and addition, which is why they belong in Grade 1 even though they feel harder.

Read, underline, solve, check

Once the type is clear, a simple four-step routine stops a child rushing to a wrong answer. Say the steps aloud together until they run on their own.

  • Read the whole problem twice — once for the story, once for the numbers.
  • Underline the two numbers and the question words (how many left, how many more, how many fewer).
  • Solve by writing a number sentence: 12 − 5 = ___, not just a scribbled answer.
  • Check that the answer makes sense — for subtraction it should be smaller than the number you started with.

That last check is the quiet hero. A child who works out 12 − 5 and writes 7 can glance back and confirm 7 is smaller than 12, so a subtraction was reasonable. It catches the ‘I added by mistake’ slip before it lands on paper.

Worked examples within 20

Here are the three types side by side, each solved the same way. Notice the number sentence is identical in shape — only the story wrapper changes.

Story typeProblemNumber sentenceAnswer
Take-awayPriya had 12 toffees; she gave away 512 − 5 = ___7 toffees
CompareRohan has 12 marbles, Sameer has 8; how many more?12 − 8 = ___4 marbles
Missing-partAarav needs 15 stickers, has 9; how many more?15 − 9 = ___6 stickers

For the ones that cross ten — 12 − 5, 15 − 9 — lean on the counting-back or bridging-through-ten habit your child already uses in plain subtraction: to do 15 − 9, take 5 to reach 10, then 4 more to reach 6. The word problem is only a costume; the arithmetic underneath is the same.

The mistake to watch for: keyword hunting

You will see it advised everywhere — ‘left’ means subtract, ‘more’ means add. It is a trap. In a compare story, ‘how many more does Rohan have?’ is a subtraction; in an add-to story, ‘4 more arrived’ is an addition. The very same word points different ways depending on the story. Keywords are a hint, never a rule. The reliable habit is the one above: work out what is actually happening — is a group shrinking, are two amounts being compared, is a missing part being found — then choose the operation. Teach the structure, not the vocabulary shortcut.

Why the numbers stay small on purpose

Every example here keeps the numbers at or below 20, and that is deliberate. In Grade 1 the reading and the reasoning are the hard part, not the calculation. If the numbers are big enough that a child struggles to subtract them, all their attention goes to the arithmetic and none is left for understanding the story. Keep subtraction within 20 for a full term of word-problem practice before you push higher. There is no prize for rushing.

Try the quiz, then the printable practice

The eight-question quiz below mixes all three story types, all within 20. Let your child read each one aloud, name the type, then pick an answer — and read the explanations together for any they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable word-problems e-book at the end gives graded story sums with a full answer key.

quiz.title: 1st Grade Subtraction Word Problems Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight short story problems mixing take-away, compare and missing-part types, all within 20. Read each one, decide the type, pick an answer, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Priya had 12 toffees. She gave 5 to her brother. How many are left?
questions.explanation: A take-away story: the group shrinks. 12 − 5 = 7. Count back from 12, or bridge through ten.

questions.q: Rohan has 12 marbles. Sameer has 8. How many more does Rohan have?
questions.explanation: A compare story: measure the gap between the two amounts. 12 − 8 = 4. Nobody lost anything — it is still a subtraction.

questions.q: Aarav needs 15 stickers to fill his chart. He has 9. How many more does he need?
questions.explanation: A missing-part story: find the piece that is missing. 15 − 9 = 6. Do not let ‘how many more’ trick you into adding.

questions.q: A basket had 14 mangoes. The family ate 6. How many are left?
questions.explanation: Take-away: 14 − 6 = 8. Bridge through ten — take 4 to reach 10, then 2 more to reach 8.

questions.q: Meera read 11 pages. Diya read 7 pages. How many fewer did Diya read?
questions.explanation: A compare story with ‘how many fewer’. 11 − 7 = 4. Comparing means finding the difference.

questions.q: Which step should you do LAST when solving a word problem?
questions.explanation: Read, underline, solve, then check. For subtraction, check the answer is smaller than the number you started with.

questions.q: Sana had 10 balloons. 3 flew away. How many does she have now?
questions.explanation: Take-away: 10 − 3 = 7. The balloons leaving the group is the subtraction.

questions.q: For any subtraction word problem, the answer should be…
options: Bigger than the number you started with
Smaller than the number you started with
questions.explanation: Taking away or finding a difference makes the result smaller than the amount you began with. That is the quick check.

faq.q: What are the three types of subtraction word problems in Grade 1?
faq.a: Take-away (something leaves a group, like toffees given away), compare (how many more or fewer one amount is than another), and missing-part (a total and one part are known, find the missing part). Naming the type first makes the subtraction obvious.

faq.q: Why does my child get subtraction word problems wrong even when their subtraction is fine?
faq.a: Because the hard part is reading, not subtracting. Compare and missing-part stories do not feel like take-away, so a child who knows 12 − 8 = 4 may not realise the story is asking for it. Teaching the three structures — and the read-underline-solve-check habit — fixes the gap.

faq.q: Why do compare stories confuse young children?
faq.a: Because nothing is taken away — two amounts just sit side by side and you measure the gap. There is no action to picture, so it does not look like subtraction. Show your child that ‘how many more’ and ‘how many fewer’ both mean find the difference.

faq.q: Are keyword tricks like ‘left means subtract’ reliable?
faq.a: No. ‘More’ sits inside both additions and subtractions — ‘4 more arrived’ is an addition, ‘how many more does he have’ is a subtraction. Teach children to picture what happens in the story rather than hunt for a magic word.
